name: The Flanders Campaign
brief: In 1793 Britain joined the First Coalition to check Revolutionary France's advance into the Low Countries, fighting alongside Austrian, Dutch and Hanoverian allies. It became a campaign of marches, sieges and hard-fought village actions rather than one decisive battle, and though it ended in a costly withdrawal, it forged a generation of British officers, Wellington among them. This campaign works well as an introduction to Napoleonic wargaming, the Battles are smaller in scale than the Peninsular fights to come, and the Operations lean on delaying actions and holding key ground rather than outright annihilation.

name: The Peninsular Campaign
brief: From 1808 Britain committed to defending Portugal and driving Napoleon's marshals out of Spain, a campaign that grew into Britain's longest and most successful of the wars under Sir Arthur Wellesley, later Wellington. Villages, ridges, bridges and mountain passes decided battles as often as raw numbers did, and small actions by riflemen and cavalry regularly determined whether whole armies survived to fight on. This is the widest-ranging of the three campaigns, moving from desperate defensive rearguards through increasingly confident offensives to the invasion of France itself.

name: The Waterloo Campaign
brief: Napoleon's escape from Elba in March 1815 forced the Seventh Coalition to move fast, and his own plan was to strike Wellington and Blücher separately before their armies could combine. What followed was only four days of campaigning, 15–18 June, but produced some of the most famous fighting in military history, as Wellington's Anglo-Allied army bought time for the Prussians to arrive. This campaign naturally alternates between the two enormous set-piece battles and the smaller, desperate actions fought around the farms and crossroads that decided them.
